clue.text: Stiff stuff made by males …

parts.note: a buck is a male deer or rabbit
a ram is a male sheep; the plural word supplies two different males

explanation.surface: A stiff fabric turned out by men, with the dots leading on into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural 'males' is used twice over: two different male animals placed side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Buckram is a coarse cloth stiffened with glue or size, used in bookbinding and to give shape to clothes.

clue.text: Insect and rodent drink a little milk, under a pint

parts.note: a bee is an insect

indicators.note: a creature that drinks takes something inside it

parts.note: a rat is a rodent

indicators.note: a little of the word means just a small piece of it, its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Pests in a pub drinking milk spilt beneath a glass of beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Under a pint' is the whole definition, not a position instruction: it names what sits beneath a glass in a pub.
explanation.definitionFit: A beer mat is the cardboard coaster placed below a glass of beer in a pub.

clue.text: City succeeding to win for another

indicators.note: succeeding means coming straight after, so we want only the part that follows the given word

parts.note: another English city, the old capital of Wessex
taken as written

explanation.surface: A city's team succeeds in winning on behalf of a rival.
explanation.walkthrough: Put WIN before the answer and you get another city, Winchester; so remove WIN from Winchester. Chester is a Roman walled city in north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Chester is a cathedral city in Cheshire, England, so the plain word City defines it by example.

clue.text: Top of range: enter Beatle

indicators.note: in a down clue the top of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the opening letter of the word
to enter is to go in; the two little words are set down as 'in go'

explanation.surface: A stage direction: from the top of the mountains, enter a Beatle.
explanation.definitionFit: Ringo Starr was the drummer of the Beatles, so the band member defines him by example.

clue.text: Spiteful male model about to get dressed

indicators.note: 'about' means going around, so the first pieces wrap round the last

parts.note: a man is a male
the Model T was Ford's famous car
soldiers dress ranks, lining up straight

explanation.surface: A catty male model, about to get dressed for a show.
explanation.walkthrough: To dress, in military drill, is to line up in neat rows; the Model T is the classic crossword model.
explanation.definitionFit: Malignant means wishing harm to others, which is what being spiteful amounts to.

clue.text: … one of whom talks about meat in coral islands

indicators.note: 'about' here means placed around, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: following on from 1 across, one of the males is a ram, and what a ram does when it talks is bleat
ham is cured pork

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: a man who chatters about food on a tropical island holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: The leading dots tie this to 1 across: 'whom' refers to the males there, and the one that talks is the sheep.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bahamas are an Atlantic archipelago of low islands built largely on coral reefs and limestone banks.

clue.text: 23down changed to one that's dyed in the wool

definitions.text: one that's dyed in the wool

parts.note: 23 down is GREAT, and great means big

indicators.note: something changed is altered in form, so the following little word is rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A great figure turned into a die-hard.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference gives a synonym, not the answer word itself; then TO is jumbled.
explanation.definitionFit: A bigot holds fixed prejudices, which fits the idiom 'dyed in the wool': unchangeable, like wool coloured before it is spun.

clue.text: Respectful of choir in trouble

indicators.note: something in trouble is disordered, so the letters before it are scrambled

parts.note: taken letter for letter, to be jumbled

explanation.surface: Speaking deferentially of a choir that has got into difficulties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In trouble' looks like one phrase, but 'in' is part of the jumbled letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Honorific describes a title or form of address that conveys respect, such as 'Sir' or 'Your Honour'.

clue.text: Girl I have reached by letter

parts.note: a miss is a young woman
the contraction I've

explanation.surface: A young woman tells of being contacted by post.
explanation.definitionFit: A missive is a written message, especially a long or formal letter.

clue.text: Turn the Guardian blue and it will stop functioning

definitions.note: the phrase describes the effect of the verb: to make something stop working

indicators.note: to turn round is to face the other way, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: the clue appeared in the Guardian, which refers to itself as 'us'
to blue money is to squander it

explanation.surface: A political threat: if the newspaper turns Tory blue, it will fold.
explanation.walkthrough: Blue as a verb is old slang for squandering money. The Guardian is the paper this puzzle ran in.
explanation.definitionFit: To suspend an activity is to halt it temporarily, so it stops working for a while.

clue.text: Queen engulfed in volcano and left for ever

indicators.note: something engulfed is swallowed up inside something else, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: Etna is the volcano in Sicily
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the usual crossword queen
L is the standard abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A queen is swallowed by an erupting volcano and abandoned there for good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like the past tense of leave, but it is the direction, abbreviated.
explanation.definitionFit: Something eternal lasts without end, which is exactly what lasting for ever describes as an adjective phrase.

clue.text: Origin of the Bible

parts.note: surface reading: where the Bible came from, how the scriptures were first compiled
setter's reading: the opening book of the Bible, whose name itself is a word for a beginning or source

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a question about how the Bible was written, but it wants the first book, whose title happens also to mean 'origin'.
explanation.definitionFit: The first book of the Old Testament tells of creation, and its name is also a general word for the beginning of anything.

clue.text: Duty on a lot of spirits? That was my idea

indicators.note: a lot of something is most but not all of it, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: meths is short for methylated spirits
what one ought to do is one's duty

explanation.surface: A tax on drink, and someone claiming credit for the policy.
explanation.walkthrough: Meths is methylated spirits; 'a lot of' trims it by one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Methought is the archaic past tense of 'methinks', meaning 'it seemed to me' or 'I thought'.

clue.text: Resurrect the god that is Egypt's head

parts.note: Ra is the ancient Egyptian sun god
taken as written

indicators.note: a word's head is its front end, so only its opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the country's name

explanation.surface: Bringing back the Egyptian god who heads the nation's pantheon.
explanation.definitionFit: To raise the dead is to bring them back to life, the biblical sense of resurrection.

clue.text: Cast hasn't finished the quarrel

indicators.note: something not finished is missing its end, so the last letter goes

parts.note: taken as written
a row is a noisy argument

explanation.surface: A theatre company is still in the middle of a backstage dispute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' looks like the theatre company, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To cast and to throw are synonyms, as in casting a stone or a fishing line.

clue.text: Writer sadly dims in value

indicators.note: 'in' places the scrambled letters inside the next word

parts.note: worth means value

indicators.note: something going sadly has gone wrong, so the word after it is scrambled

parts.note: taken as written, to be jumbled

explanation.surface: An author's market value sadly fades.
explanation.definitionFit: A wordsmith is a skilled user of words, an informal term for a writer.

clue.text: For 23down 24 no beer in the Arndale Centre's the chief worry

indicators.note: 'Centre's' reads as 'centre is', placing the jumbled word in the middle
'no' says the following item is taken away from the name it sits in

parts.note: the Arndale Centre is a shopping centre in Manchester
ale is a type of beer

indicators.note: to worry something is to tug and shake it about, so its letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, to be jumbled

explanation.surface: In a shopping centre with no pub, the manager's main concern is the lack of beer.
explanation.walkthrough: ARNDALE without ALE leaves ARND; a jumble of CHIEF goes into its centre. The Arndale Centre is a big Manchester mall, bombed by the IRA in 1996.
explanation.definitionFit: The Great Satan is the Devil himself, and archfiend is a traditional title for the chief of devils, used by Milton.

clue.text: Fellow member according to law knowing what goes on?

parts.note: co- means joint or fellow, as in co-worker
an MP is a Member of Parliament
licit means lawful

explanation.surface: A fellow MP who keeps within the law but knows what goes on behind the scenes.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the definition is loose: being in on wrongdoing, not merely aware.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone complicit is involved in wrongdoing, typically by knowing about it and doing nothing to stop it.

clue.text: Forest destroyer's regularity sounds a mathematical concept

indicators.note: 'sounds' tells us to listen to the words spoken rather than read them

parts.note: a logger fells trees for timber
rhythm is a regular repeated pattern

explanation.surface: The steady pace of a tree-feller's work is likened to a mathematical idea.
explanation.definitionFit: A logarithm is the power to which a base must be raised to produce a given number, a key idea in mathematics.

clue.text: Delay about building of Dome — help needed with stile

indicators.note: 'about' sets the first word around what follows

parts.note: a lag is a delay

indicators.note: building something assembles it afresh, so the letters are put together in a new order

parts.note: the Millennium Dome in London, its letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Building the Millennium Dome is behind schedule and needs a hand.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb is 'to help a lame dog over a stile', meaning to assist someone in difficulty; a stile is a set of steps over a farm fence.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb about helping a lame dog over a stile makes the injured animal the one who needs help to climb over.

clue.text: Forbidding the writer (Conan Doyle) a burial place on Dartmoor

parts.note: grim means stern and forbidding
a writer's tool stands for the writer

explanation.surface: A writer on bleak Dartmoor, as Conan Doyle was when he set a tale there.
explanation.walkthrough: Grimpen Mire is the deadly bog in Conan Doyle's 'The Hound of the Baskervilles'; Dartmoor is moorland in Devon.
explanation.definitionFit: In the novel the Grimpen Mire swallows animals and finally the villain Stapleton, so it is the place where things are buried.

clue.text: Conservative member to 12 himself

definitions.note: with 12 across solved, this reads 'to raise himself'

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative
a limb is a member of the body

explanation.surface: A Tory MP trying to get himself promoted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' suggests a Member of Parliament, but it means an arm or leg.
explanation.definitionFit: To climb is to haul oneself upwards, so raising himself is what a climber does.

clue.text: Press for time? It's early days

parts.note: to iron clothes is to press them
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: Pushing for more time on a project that has barely begun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press for time' sounds like urgency, but it is two separate words.
explanation.definitionFit: The Iron Age is an early period of human prehistory, when tools were first made of iron.

clue.text: Interrupt a burglary?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to cut into a conversation
second meaning: a forced entry into a building to steal

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark suggests stopping a burglary in progress, but the two parts are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means to butt into talk, and the hyphenated noun is an illegal entry into premises.

clue.text: Utility supplies hands across the Channel

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the piped or wired public supply of water, gas or electricity
second meaning: the French word for hands

explanation.walkthrough: 'Across the Channel' means in France, so the French word is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: The mains are the household connection to the public grid or water network, and in French the plural of 'main' means hands.

clue.text: Unwanted growth has proceeded round the whole street

indicators.note: 'round' places one piece encircling the others

parts.note: one who has proceeded has gone
all is the whole
St is the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: A tumour that has spread round an entire street, like an epidemic.
explanation.definitionFit: A gallstone is a hard mass formed in the gall bladder, an unwelcome lump the body grows.

clue.text: Take Oxford course (a bit of Browning?) for a jaundiced view of America

parts.note: Greats is the Oxford degree course in classics
a tan is a bit of browning by the sun; the question mark admits the poet Browning is a decoy

explanation.surface: Studying the poet Browning at Oxford gives a student a sour opinion of the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: Browning is the Victorian poet a student might read, but here it is skin browning in the sun.
explanation.definitionFit: Great Satan is the hostile name Iranian revolutionaries gave the United States, a bitterly negative label for the country.

clue.text: Cause lack of prefabrication in place of disrepute

indicators.note: 'in' puts the jumbled letters inside the word for the seedy place

parts.note: a dive is a seedy bar or club
split as PRE plus fabrication: the fabrication, something made up, reworks the three letters before it

explanation.surface: Prefabricated housing put on a rough estate leaves people in need.
explanation.walkthrough: The long word must be split in two: its tail is the instruction to rework its head.
explanation.definitionFit: To deprive someone is to take something away from them, causing them to lack it.

clue.text: Model place in Kipling's tale by himself

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the runway on which fashion models parade
second meaning: the Just So Story 'The Cat that Walked by Himself', read as the feline taking a stroll

explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's Just So Stories include 'The Cat that Walked by Himself'; the clue squeezes that title into the two words of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A catwalk is the narrow raised stage where models show clothes; in Kipling's story the cat famously goes walking on its own.

clue.text: Return cosy and glowing from report

indicators.note: to return is to go back the way one came, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: snug means warm and cosy
something glowing is hot

explanation.surface: Coming back warm and contented from a news story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Report' looks like a news piece, but here it is the loud bang of a gun.
explanation.definitionFit: A report is an explosive noise, the sound of a gun firing.

clue.text: What Internet users produce is ruin

indicators.note: what the run of words produces is a string sitting across the word boundary

parts.note: the letters run from the end of the first word into the second

explanation.surface: Online users are blamed for wrecking something.
explanation.walkthrough: Tintern Abbey is a ruined Cistercian abbey in the Wye valley in Wales, the subject of a Wordsworth poem.
explanation.definitionFit: Tintern Abbey is one of Britain's most celebrated ruins, so the place name stands for a ruin by example.
